lessonTitle: Preoperative Assessment: Risk, Consent and Medicines

blocks.text: A 76-year-old man is listed for a right hemicolectomy on Thursday. His medication list reads: warfarin for atrial fibrillation, metformin for type 2 diabetes, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for the past two years. None of these can simply be taken or stopped on the morning of surgery, and getting any one of them wrong can cause a bleed, an acute illness or an adrenal crisis.

blocks.markdown: Preoperative assessment has four aims: to establish what is wrong and whether surgery is the right option, to estimate and reduce the patient's perioperative risk, to obtain valid informed consent, and to plan the safe management of medicines and comorbidities. Risk is the product of **patient factors** and **procedure factors**, and a good assessment makes both explicit so that the patient and team can decide together.

blocks.caption: Patient and procedure factors that raise perioperative risk
rows: Reduced physiological reserve, delirium, longer recovery
Ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, arrhythmia, valve disease
Chronic kidney disease, diabetes, obesity (BMI of 30 or more)
Acute kidney injury, infection, wound and anaesthetic difficulty
Unable to manage about 4 metabolic equivalents (cannot climb two flights of stairs)
Emergency rather than elective; major, long, or intraperitoneal, intrathoracic or vascular surgery; high blood loss

blocks.title: ASA physical status
blocks.text: The American Society of Anesthesiologists grade describes overall health: ASA I a normal healthy patient; ASA II mild systemic disease without functional limitation (e.g. well-controlled hypertension or diabetes, smoker); ASA III severe systemic disease with functional limitation (e.g. poorly controlled diabetes, COPD, stable angina); ASA IV severe disease that is a constant threat to life (e.g. recent myocardial infarction, sepsis); ASA V moribund and not expected to survive without surgery; ASA VI brain-dead organ donor. An 'E' is added for emergency surgery.

blocks.caption: Body mass index: 30 kg/m2 or more is obesity, 40 or more is class III. Obesity increases anaesthetic difficulty and wound and thromboembolic complications.

blocks.markdown: **The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI)** gives one point for each of six factors: high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic or suprainguinal vascular), ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, and serum creatinine above 177 micromol/L (2.0 mg/dL). The risk of major cardiac complications rises stepwise with the score (0, 1, 2, 3 or more), and a high score prompts optimisation, a discussion of alternatives and a higher level of postoperative care.

blocks.title: Calculating the RCRI
blocks.prompt: A 70-year-old man with heart failure and diet-controlled diabetes is booked for an open sigmoid colectomy. His creatinine is 198 micromol/L and he has no history of angina, myocardial infarction or stroke. What is his RCRI score?

steps.text: Open sigmoid colectomy is intraperitoneal surgery: high-risk surgery, 1 point.
Heart failure: 1 point. No ischaemic heart disease and no cerebrovascular disease: 0 points.
Diabetes counts only if treated with insulin, and his is diet-controlled: 0 points.

blocks.answer: RCRI 3: high risk of major cardiac complications, so optimise heart failure and renal function, discuss risk with the patient, and plan high-dependency postoperative care.

blocks.markdown: **Valid informed consent** has four elements: the patient must have **capacity** (able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate a decision; presumed unless shown otherwise), the decision must be **voluntary** (free from pressure), they must be given **adequate information** (the nature of the procedure, its benefits, material risks, alternatives including doing nothing, and what recovery involves), and the consenting clinician must be trained and competent in the procedure or suitably supervised. The legal standard in the UK (the Montgomery judgment) is that a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or if the clinician knows the particular patient would. The signed form records consent but is not itself consent; it is a process of discussion. If a patient lacks capacity, decisions are made in their best interests under the Mental Capacity Act, consulting those close to them.

blocks.title: Materiality is about the patient, not the percentage
blocks.text: A 1 in 100 risk of nerve injury is trivial to some patients and career-ending to a musician. Material risks are determined by what matters to this patient, not by a fixed threshold.

blocks.caption: Preparing patients on high-risk medicines (follow local protocol)
rows: Stop in time for the INR to fall
Stop about 5 days before; check INR the day before (aim below about 1.5); bridging with heparin only for very high thrombotic risk
Omit for a period depending on bleeding risk and renal function
Omit roughly 1 day before low-bleeding-risk and 2 days before high-bleeding-risk surgery with normal renal function; longer if renal impairment
Never omit all insulin in type 1 diabetes; keep glucose controlled
Adjust dose or use a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion when fasting is prolonged
Avoid hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis
Omit sulfonylureas on the morning of surgery; withhold SGLT2 inhibitors for the interval specified in local guidance because of the risk of euglycaemic ketoacidosis; follow local metformin policy
Long-term use suppresses the adrenal axis
Never stop abruptly; give extra stress-dose hydrocortisone (e.g. 100 mg intravenously at induction for major surgery, as a teaching example) per local protocol

blocks.title: Planning a warfarin patient for elective surgery
blocks.prompt: A 69-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation with no previous stroke (low to moderate thrombotic risk) is booked for elective hernia repair on a Friday. How do you plan anticoagulation?

steps.text: Stop warfarin 5 days before surgery, which is Sunday, so that the INR falls to a safe level.
Bridging with heparin is not needed for atrial fibrillation without recent stroke; it is reserved for very high thrombotic risk (such as a mechanical mitral valve).
Check the INR the day before or on the day of surgery; proceed if below about 1.5, otherwise discuss and consider low-dose oral vitamin K.
Restart warfarin that evening or the next day once haemostasis is secure, with an INR check after a few days.

blocks.answer: Stop warfarin 5 days earlier, no bridging, confirm INR below about 1.5 before surgery, and restart afterwards when bleeding risk allows.

blocks.title: Do not stop long-term steroids
blocks.text: Patients taking prednisolone at doses of about 5 mg daily or more for several weeks may have suppressed adrenal responses. Missing doses or failing to provide stress-dose steroid cover can cause hypotension, hypoglycaemia and adrenal crisis under the physiological stress of surgery.

points: Perioperative risk reflects patient factors (age, cardiac, respiratory, renal, diabetes, obesity, functional capacity) and procedure factors (urgency, magnitude, site).
ASA grade and tools such as the Revised Cardiac Risk Index structure risk estimation, and BMI quantifies obesity.
Valid consent needs capacity, voluntariness, adequate information including material risks and alternatives, and a competent consenter.
Anticoagulants, antidiabetics and steroids each need a planned approach: timed omission, controlled glucose, and never abruptly stopping long-term steroids.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with well-controlled hypertension and no functional limitation is listed for an elective inguinal hernia repair. What is his ASA grade?

options.text: ASA II
ASA I
ASA III
ASA IV

distractorRationale.a: Correct: mild, well-controlled systemic disease without limitation.
distractorRationale.b: ASA I implies a normal healthy patient with no disease.
distractorRationale.c: ASA III needs severe systemic disease with functional limitation.
distractorRationale.d: ASA IV is a constant threat to life.

questions.explanation: Well-controlled hypertension without functional limitation is a mild systemic disease, which defines ASA II. Higher grades require disease that limits function or threatens life.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a procedure-related factor that increases perioperative risk?

options.text: Emergency rather than elective surgery
A history of smoking
Age over 75
Insulin-treated diabetes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: emergency status describes the procedure and context; the patient is less optimised.

questions.explanation: Procedure factors include urgency, extent, duration and site of the operation. Emergency surgery carries higher risk because there is little time to optimise the patient.

questions.stem: A patient is handed a consent form to sign in the anaesthetic room while already sedated with a premedication, after a surgeon they have not previously met mentions the operation briefly. Why is this consent likely to be invalid?

options.text: Capacity may be impaired by sedation and there has been no adequate information, risks or alternatives discussion
Consent must always be witnessed by a family member
Consent must be obtained by the consultant only
Written consent is never valid in an anaesthetic room

questions.correctOptionText: Capacity may be impaired by sedation and there has been no adequate information, risks or alternatives discussion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: valid consent needs capacity and adequate information, and is a process not a signature.
distractorRationale.b: A family witness is not required.
distractorRationale.c: Any suitably trained clinician can take consent, not only the consultant.
distractorRationale.d: The location alone does not invalidate consent; the circumstances do.

questions.explanation: Valid consent requires capacity, voluntariness and adequate information, none of which is secured by signing a form while sedated after a brief mention. The consent discussion should happen well before, with time to ask questions.

questions.stem: A professional violinist is being consented for carpal tunnel decompression, which carries about a 1% risk of persistent numbness of the fingertips. The surgeon decides not to mention it because the risk is low. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The risk is material for this patient, because a reasonable person in her position, and this patient in particular, would attach significance to it, so it should be disclosed
Risks below 5% never need to be disclosed
Only risks that the surgeon considers significant need to be mentioned
The risk need only be disclosed if the patient asks

questions.correctOptionText: The risk is material for this patient, because a reasonable person in her position, and this patient in particular, would attach significance to it, so it should be disclosed

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the materiality test depends on the patient's circumstances.
distractorRationale.c: The test is not what the surgeon thinks is significant.
distractorRationale.d: The clinician must volunteer material risks.

questions.explanation: The legal and professional standard turns on what the particular patient, or a reasonable person in their position, would consider important. For a violinist, fingertip numbness is highly significant even at low probability.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and is listed for an elective colectomy. Which plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop warfarin about 5 days before and give heparin bridging because his thrombotic risk is very high, with the INR checked before surgery
Continue warfarin unchanged with an INR of 3.5
Stop warfarin the evening before only
Stop warfarin and give no anticoagulation of any kind until discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Stop warfarin about 5 days before and give heparin bridging because his thrombotic risk is very high, with the INR checked before surgery

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a mechanical mitral valve is a very high thrombotic risk, so bridging covers the period of subtherapeutic INR.
distractorRationale.b: A high INR risks serious surgical bleeding.
distractorRationale.c: One day is insufficient for the INR to fall.
distractorRationale.d: Leaving a mechanical mitral valve unprotected risks valve thrombosis and stroke.

questions.explanation: Warfarin is stopped about 5 days beforehand so the INR falls, but a mechanical mitral valve carries a very high thrombotic risk, so therapeutic heparin bridges the gap. Bridging is not routine for lower-risk indications such as atrial fibrillation without prior stroke because it increases bleeding.

questions.stem: A patient taking long-term prednisolone should stop it before surgery to reduce infection risk.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal axis, and abrupt withdrawal or missed perioperative cover can cause adrenal crisis. Steroids are continued, with additional stress-dose cover for major surgery per local protocol.

questions.stem: A man weighing 118 kg and 1.72 m tall is assessed before bariatric surgery. Calculate his body mass index in kg/m2 (to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: BMI is weight divided by height squared: 1.72^2 = 2.9584, and 118 / 2.9584 = 39.9 kg/m2. This is just below the class III obesity threshold of 40, still conferring higher anaesthetic and wound risk.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is listed for an open anterior resection (intraperitoneal surgery). She had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago, has had a transient ischaemic attack, takes insulin for diabetes, and has no heart failure. Her creatinine is 130 micromol/L. Using the Revised Cardiac Risk Index in the lesson, what is her score (points)?
questions.explanation: High-risk (intraperitoneal) surgery scores 1, ischaemic heart disease from the myocardial infarction scores 1, cerebrovascular disease from the TIA scores 1, and insulin-treated diabetes scores 1. Heart failure is absent and creatinine 130 is below 177 micromol/L, so the total is 4.

questions.stem: List and explain the elements of valid informed consent for surgery, and describe how you would proceed if the patient lacks capacity.
markingGuide: Capacity: understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision; presumed unless shown otherwise
Voluntariness: free from coercion or undue pressure
Information: nature of procedure, benefits, material risks, alternatives including no treatment
Materiality tested by what a reasonable person in the patient's position, or this patient, would consider significant
Consenting clinician competent and consent is a process, the form records it
Lack of capacity: act in the patient's best interests under the Mental Capacity Act, consult family or carers and any advance decisions or attorney
Emergency treatment may proceed in best interests if delay would cause serious harm
questions.explanation: Valid consent depends on a competent, uncoerced patient who is told what a reasonable patient would want to know. Where capacity is lacking, decisions follow a structured best-interests process.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on apixaban, metformin and long-term prednisolone is listed for elective major abdominal surgery. Outline how you would prepare her for each of these medicines and the risks of getting each wrong.
markingGuide: DOAC: omit for a period guided by bleeding risk and renal function (roughly 1 day low-risk, 2 days high-risk with normal renal function), follow local protocol; risk of surgical bleeding or neuraxial haematoma if not stopped
Bridging usually not needed with DOACs
Metformin: follow local policy, especially with renal impairment or contrast, because of lactic acidosis risk
Monitor glucose, avoid prolonged hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia
Prednisolone: continue and do not stop abruptly; stress-dose hydrocortisone cover for major surgery
Risk of omission: adrenal crisis with hypotension and hypoglycaemia
Plan documented, communicated to anaesthetist and patient, and restart timing specified
questions.explanation: Each drug class has a different perioperative hazard: bleeding for anticoagulants, metabolic derangement for antidiabetics and adrenal crisis for steroids. A written plan with timing and restart instructions reduces avoidable harm.
